rationale: Eliphaz says that those who sow improper things perish by the Lord's command and the breath of His anger. The letter says the Lord Jesus will kill the lawless one with the breath of His mouth. Both employ the Lord's breath as the means of overthrow, but Eliphaz's claim is not a verdict that Job is guilty, nor are his unnamed offenders identified with the letter's lawless one.
source_text: By the Lord’s command they will perish; by the breath of His anger they will disappear.

target_units.text: And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of His mouth and bring to nothing by the manifestation of His coming.

relationship: Audible speech without a visible form
rationale: Eliphaz reports hearing a breeze and a voice while seeing no form and not recognizing the presence. Deuteronomy recalls Israel hearing words but seeing no likeness at Horeb, only a voice. The shared feature is heard speech without a visible form; Deuteronomy explicitly names the Lord as speaker, and that identity or authority is not transferred to Eliphaz's unrecognized presence.
source_text: I stood up and did not recognize it; I looked, and there was no form before my eyes, but I heard a breeze and a voice:

target_units.text: And the Lord spoke unto you out of the midst of the fire; you heard the sound of words, but saw no likeness, only a voice.

relationship: Righteous benefit contrasted with the loss of the impious
rationale: Eliphaz's account moves from fools' ruined way of life to the righteous eating gathered goods. Proverbs explicitly says that the wealth of the impious is stored up for the righteous. Both place the righteous person's benefit beside wrongdoing's loss. The source's pronouns are not used to identify particular owners or a transaction, and the proverb does not identify Job's lost property or endorse Eliphaz's application to him.
source_text: For the righteous will eat what they gathered, and they themselves will not be rescued from evils; may their strength be drained away.

target_units.text: A good man will inherit children’s children, but the wealth of the impious is stored up for the righteous.

relationship: Lament over help remaining far away
rationale: Job contrasts his trust with help being far from him. The psalm directly asks the Lord not to put the speaker's help far away and to attend to his support. Both express distress through the distance of help, with Job stating his experienced lack and the psalm petitioning against it; the psalm's later claim that God heard the petition is not inserted into Job's present complaint.
source_text: Had I not trusted in Him? But help is far from me.

target_units.text: But Thou, Lord, do not put my help far away; attend to my support.

relationship: Petition for relief before departure from life
rationale: Job asks for his wrongdoing to be forgotten and his sin cleansed before he departs into the earth and is no more. The psalm asks the Lord to hear and grant relief before the speaker departs and no longer exists. Both make anticipated departure the urgent setting for a petition, while Job's request for cleansing and the psalm's request for refreshment remain distinct.
source_text: Why hast Thou not brought about forgetfulness of my lawlessness and cleansing of my sin? But now I will depart into the earth; at daybreak I am no more.”

target_units.text: Hear my prayer, Lord, and give ear to my supplication; do not remain silent at my tears. For I am a sojourner with Thee and a temporary resident like all my fathers.
Give me relief, that I may be refreshed, before I depart and no longer exist.”

rationale: Job asks who grew hard against the mighty God and endured. Romans voices an imagined objection asking who has resisted God's purpose, then challenges a human being's answering back to God. Both formulate divine-human resistance as a rhetorical question. Job's complaint and Paul's reply to an objector are different arguments; neither identifies Job with Pharaoh or endorses every inference of the other speaker.
source_text: For He is wise in understanding, mighty and great. Who grew hard against Him and endured?

target_units.text: You will then say to me, “Why, then, does He still find fault? For who has resisted His purpose?”
But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is formed say to the One who formed it, “Why didst Thou make me this way?”

relationship: Darkness and the land of the dead in lament
rationale: Job describes the land to which he expects to go as without brightness or sight of mortal life. The psalm asks whether mercy is recounted in the grave or wonders known in darkness and a forgotten land. Both laments associate death with a dark land cut off from ordinary living experience; the comparison preserves their lamenting voices and does not construct a complete account of the afterlife.
source_text: to a land of everlasting darkness, where there is no brightness and no seeing the life of mortals.’”

target_units.text: Surely no one will recount Thy mercy in a grave and Thy truth in destruction?
Surely Thy wonders will not be known in darkness, or Thy righteousness in a forgotten land?

rationale: Job asks who could rebuild what God throws down or open what He shuts. In Isaiah the Lord declares that no one rescues from His hands and asks who will turn back His action. Both deny a human capacity to undo God's act. Isaiah does not supply Job's particular demolition or confinement images, and no specific prisoner or destroyed building is identified.
source_text: If He throws down, who will build? If He shuts people in, who will open?

target_units.text: still from the beginning. No one rescues from My hands. I will act, and who will turn it back?”

relationship: Wind-carried leaves as an image of vulnerability
rationale: Job asks why God would oppose one as frail as a wind-moved leaf or grass carried by a breeze. Isaiah's communal confession depicts people falling like leaves and being carried off by wind because of their lawless deeds. The shared plant-and-wind image expresses vulnerability, while the confession's stated guilt is not imposed on Job's plea.
source_text: Wilt Thou be wary of a leaf moved by wind, or oppose me as grass carried by a breeze?

target_units.text: We all became like unclean people; all our righteousness is like a menstruating woman’s rag. We fell away like leaves because of our lawless deeds; thus wind will carry us off.

rationale: Eliphaz portrays the ungodly person's life as anxiety. Isaiah pictures the unjust as wave-tossed and unable to rest, and declares no rejoicing for the ungodly. Both associate wrongdoing with unrest, but the prophetic statement does not prove Eliphaz's insinuation that Job's suffering establishes his guilt.
source_text: An ungodly person’s whole life is in anxiety, and numbered years are given to a ruler.

target_units.text: But the unjust will be tossed by waves in this way and will be unable to rest.
‘There is no rejoicing for the ungodly,’ said the Lord God.”

relationship: Speech and silence in the experience of pain
rationale: Job says that if he speaks he will not feel pain from the wound and asks how silence would leave him any less wounded. The psalm reports that silence renewed the speaker's pain before he spoke. Both set the decision to speak against the inability of silence to remove distress; Job's conditional statement about speaking is preserved rather than changed to its opposite.
source_text: For if I speak, I will not feel pain from the wound; and if I remain silent, how will I be wounded any less?

target_units.text: I became mute and was humbled and kept silent from good things, and my pain was renewed.
My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire will be kindled. I spoke with my tongue:

relationship: Appeal to a witness beyond human observation
rationale: Job claims a witness in the heavens and one who knows with him in the highest places as he seeks a hearing. Paul calls God his witness to the unceasing remembrance expressed in his prayers. Both appeal beyond human observation for knowledge of the speaker's case or inward practice. Job's witness remains unnamed; this comparison does not identify that figure as Christ, an angel, or Paul's explicitly named witness.
source_text: Even now, behold, my witness is in the heavens, and the one who knows with me is in the highest places.

target_units.text: For God, whom I serve in my spirit in the gospel of His Son, is my witness that I remember you without ceasing,
always in my prayers asking whether somehow now at last I may be granted a way, by the will of God, to come to you.

rationale: Job calls death his father and decay his mother and sister within his lament about Hades as his house. Proverbs tells the learner to call wisdom a sister and acquire understanding as a familiar companion. Both express closeness to an abstract reality through family language, with Job's desolate association with death contrasted with the instruction to embrace protective wisdom; these are not claims about literal relatives.
source_text: I called upon death to be my father, and decay to be my mother and sister.

target_units.text: Say that wisdom is your sister, and acquire understanding as your familiar companion,

relationship: Dispossession of houses in judgment language
rationale: Bildad says that the unjust person's house will not be preserved and that others will live in what was his. Jeremiah announces that houses, fields and wives will be transferred to others when the Lord stretches out His hand against the land's inhabitants. Both portray judgment through loss of the household to others; Jeremiah does not verify Bildad's application to Job, and neither passage is rewritten as a claim about absent descendants.
source_text: He will not be recognized among his people, nor will his house be preserved beneath heaven, but others will live in what was his.

target_units.text: And their houses will be transferred to others, fields and their wives together, because I will stretch out My hand against those dwelling in this land, says the Lord.

relationship: The lost crown as an image of humiliation
rationale: Job says that glory has been stripped from him and the crown taken from his head. Lamentations declares that the crown has fallen from the community's head. Both portray lost dignity through the crown's removal, but Lamentations' explicit confession of sin is not transferred to Job or used to identify his crown as a literal royal office.
source_text: He stripped glory from me and took the crown from my head.

target_units.text: The crown fell from our head; woe indeed to us, for we sinned!

relationship: Becoming foreign within one's own close circle
rationale: Job says that the neighbors of his house and his maidservants regard him as a foreigner. The psalm's speaker has become estranged from his brothers and a foreigner to his mother's sons. Both express painful alienation from people who should be close through foreigner language; the household members and causes are distinct, and neither statement establishes a change of ethnicity.
source_text: Neighbors of the house and my maidservants— I was a foreigner before them.

target_units.text: I became estranged from my brothers and a foreigner to my mother’s sons,

relationship: The overthrow of a house in retributive wisdom
rationale: Zophar wishes for destruction to drag the ungodly person's house away on a day of wrath. Proverbs says that the Lord pulls down the houses of the insolent while establishing a widow's boundary. Both connect wrongdoing with the loss of a house, but the proverb's principle does not establish Zophar's accusation against Job or identify either statement with the prologue's house collapse.
source_text: May destruction drag his house utterly away; may a day of wrath come upon him.

target_units.text: The Lord pulls down the houses of the insolent, but He established the boundary of a widow.
